mainTopic: Praying daily for the sick, the משנה's ruling on thick porridge, and stories about porridge and about רבי יהודה's health, simple life and poverty
overview: The amud opens by asking whose opinion we follow when we pray every day for the sick. The answer is רבי יוסי, who holds that people are judged every day, and the wording of the prayer teaches that מריעי refers to the רבנן. The גמרא then returns to the משנה's rule that someone who vowed off pot-cooked food may still eat a thick dish. It notes that this does not match the Babylonians, who eat thick porridge together with bread. This leads to a string of stories about porridge: which bread goes best with it, eating it with the fingers or with a fork, how far it is worth traveling for it, and when you may spit it out even before a king. Next come stories about רבי יהודה. He ate hard-to-digest figs, explained his healthy face by beets, wisdom and good digestion, and rejected accusations of drinking and of earning forbidden money. He and רבי שמעון carried loads to show that work brings honor, and he made a joyful ברכה over the one cloak he shared with his wife. The amud ends with רבי יהודה refusing a cloak that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל sent him for a public fast, and the story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Whose view supports praying daily for the sick?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא's opinion is behind our daily prayer for the sick and the suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion are we following when we pray for the sick and for the suffering?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a quick background question: our daily prayer for sick people matches which opinion? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Praying every day for the sick only makes sense if a person's fate can be decided on any day, not just once a year. So the גמרא wants to know which opinion holds that view.

phrases.english: In accordance with whom do we pray
for the sick and for the suffering?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a short side topic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which opinion supports praying for the sick every day.

steps.title: The answer: like רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: Our daily prayer for the sick follows רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion? רבי יוסי's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. The practice follows רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי holds that a person is judged every day. That is why it makes sense to pray for the sick every day.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who holds that people are judged every day

phrases.english: [In accordance with whom? In accordance with Rabbi Yosei.]
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have these words; the square brackets show they belong in the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The daily prayer follows רבי יוסי.

steps.title: Two words, two groups: the sick and the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: Because the prayer names both קצירי and מריעי, the גמרא learns that they are two different groups: truly sick people, and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the prayer says both 'the sick' and 'the suffering,' we learn that 'the sick' means people who are actually sick, and 'the suffering' means the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a lesson from the wording of the prayer. Two words are used, so they must mean two different groups.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both words meant 'sick,' one of them would be extra. So קצירי means the truly ill, and מריעי means the רבנן, who are often weak.
steps.whatToRemember: The daily prayer for the sick follows רבי יוסי. Its word מריעי refers to the רבנן.

phrases.english: From the fact that he said 'the sick and the suffering,'
learn from it: 'the sick' means actually sick people,
'the suffering' means the Sages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an extra lesson from the wording of the prayer just discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קצירי means the actually sick, and מריעי means the רבנן.

steps.title: The משנה's rule on thick porridge is not the Babylonian custom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that someone who vowed off pot-cooked food may still eat a thick dish, and says this ruling does not match the Babylonian custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'and he is permitted to eat a thick dish.' Our משנה does not follow the Babylonians.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about vows and quotes its words 'and he is permitted with a thick one.' It says this ruling does not fit Babylonian eating habits, and the next step explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vows follow how people usually speak and eat. In the משנה's setting, a thick dish is not counted as 'pot-cooked food,' so it stays permitted. Among the Babylonians that would not be true.

phrases.english: And he is permitted with a thick one.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: someone who vowed off loose pot-cooked food may still eat a thick dish.

phrases.english: Our mishna is not in accordance with the Babylonians,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side topic to the משנה's ruling about vows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Permitting a thick dish fits a place where it is not treated as pot food, which is not the Babylonian custom.

steps.title: רבי זירא: Babylonians eat bread with bread
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא's remark shows that Babylonians eat thick porridge together with their bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי זירא said: The Babylonians are foolish, because they eat bread with bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the previous step with a teasing remark by רבי זירא about how Babylonians eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thick porridge is so much like bread that eating it with bread is like eating 'bread with bread.' For Babylonians, though, thick porridge is a side dish, so it would count as pot food. That is why the משנה's ruling does not fit them.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who moved from Babylonia to ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: as Rabbi Zeira said: Babylonians are foolish,
for they eat bread with bread.
phrases.notes: The 'second bread' is the thick porridge, which is so filling that it is almost like bread.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim that the משנה is not like the Babylonians.
steps.raayaObject: That Babylonians treat thick porridge as a side dish eaten with bread.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי זירא's remark that Babylonians eat bread with bread.

steps.title: רב חסדא's question to the people of הוצל
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא reports a question put to the careful people of הוצל: which bread goes best with which porridge?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Let someone ask those precise people of הוצל: What is the best way to eat this porridge? Wheat porridge with wheat bread, and barley porridge with barley bread? Or maybe wheat porridge with barley bread, and barley porridge with wheat bread?
steps.whatsHappening: Still talking about eating porridge with bread, רב חסדא raises a practical question about which combination is best. The גמרא records no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the Babylonians do eat porridge with bread, the question is how to do it best. Is it better to match the grain, or to mix them? The people of הוצל were known for being exact, so the question was put to them.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said:
let someone ask those precise people of Huzal:
This porridge, how is it best to eat it?
Wheat porridge with wheat bread,
and barley porridge with barley bread,
or perhaps wheat porridge with barley bread,
and barley porridge with wheat bread?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: דִּמְשַׁאֵיל לְהוֹן לְהָלֵין נַקְדָּנֵי דְּהוּצַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the Babylonian habit of eating porridge with bread.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether porridge is best eaten with bread of the same grain or of the other grain.

steps.title: How רבא ate it
steps.stepSummary: רבא would eat it with חסיסי, a dish of toasted grains.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא would eat it with חסיסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how one חכם, רבא, actually ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of just leaving the question open, the גמרא shows real-life practice. רבא's chosen pairing was with חסיסי.

keyTerms.meaning: A dish made of toasted grains

phrases.english: Rava would eat it with ḥasisei.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a real-life example of how a חכם ate.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא's practice was to eat it with חסיסי.

steps.title: Why is רב הונא eating with his fingers?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא finds his father רב הונא eating porridge with his fingers and asks why.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא found רב הונא eating porridge with his fingers. He asked him: Why is the master eating with his hand?
steps.whatsHappening: A story begins. A son is surprised to see his father eating porridge by hand, and he asks why. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating porridge by hand looks improper, especially for a great חכם. The question invites an explanation of why רב הונא does it.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ לְרַב הוּנָא
phrases.english: Rabba, son of Rav Huna, found Rav Huna
eating porridge with his fingers.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי קָאָכֵיל מָר בִּידֵיהּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why is the master eating with his hand?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַמַּאי קָאָכֵיל מָר בִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another story about eating porridge.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב הונא eats porridge with his hand.

steps.title: רב: porridge tastes better by hand
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא quotes רב: porridge is tasty when eaten with one finger, even more so with two, and even more so with three.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is what רב said: Porridge eaten with a finger is tasty, all the more so with two fingers, and all the more so with three.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers his son by quoting his teacher רב. Eating porridge by hand makes it taste better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He was not being careless. He was following רב's teaching that porridge is more enjoyable when eaten with the fingers, and the more fingers, the better.
steps.whatToRemember: These stories about porridge come from the משנה's rule about thick dishes. רב teaches that porridge is tastier eaten by hand.

phrases.english: He said to him: This is what Rav said:
Porridge with a finger is tasty,
and all the more so with two,
and all the more so with three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the son's question in step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב taught that porridge tastes better eaten with the fingers, and better still with more fingers.

steps.title: How far to travel for porridge and for ox meat
steps.stepSummary: רב and רב הונא tell their sons: for a porridge meal, travel up to one פרסה; for ox meat, up to three פרסאות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב told his son חייא, and רב הונא told his son רבה the same thing: If you are invited to eat porridge, it is worth going up to a parasang. To eat ox meat, it is worth going up to three parasangs.
steps.whatsHappening: Two fathers give their sons the same practical advice about how far a good meal is worth traveling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the praise of porridge from the earlier steps. Porridge is worth a trip of one פרסה, and ox meat, which is even better, is worth three times that distance.

keyTerms.meaning: A parasang, a unit of distance (roughly 4 km)

phrases.english: Rav said to his son Chiyya,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא לְרַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ:
phrases.english: and Rav Huna likewise said to his son Rabba:

phrases.aramaic: מְזַמְּנִים לָךְ לְמֵיכַל דַּיְיסָא עַד פַּרְסָה.
phrases.english: If you are invited to eat porridge, go up to a parasang.

phrases.aramaic: לְמֵיכַל בִּישְׂרָא דְתוֹרָא עַד תְּלָתָא פַּרְסִין.
phrases.english: To eat ox meat, go up to three parasangs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב לְחִיָּיא בְּרֵיהּ, וְכֵן אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא לְרַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the praise of porridge, now measured by how far it is worth traveling to eat it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A porridge meal is worth a journey of one פרסה; ox meat is worth three פרסאות.

steps.title: Do not spit before your teacher, except gourd and porridge
steps.stepSummary: The same fathers teach that you may not spit out food in front of your teacher, except gourd and porridge, which are dangerous to swallow if they will not go down well. Those you spit out even before the king.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב told his son חייא, and רב הונא told his son רבה the same thing: Do not spit out anything in front of your teacher, except gourd and porridge, because they are like a lead wick. Spit those out even in front of שבור מלכא.
steps.whatsHappening: A second piece of advice from the same two fathers: a rule of respect toward your teacher, with an exception for two foods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, spitting out food in front of your רבי is disrespectful. Gourd and porridge are an exception, because swallowing them when they will not go down well is like swallowing a burning lead wick. Health comes before honor, even the honor of a king.

keyTerms.meaning: A wick of lead (something dangerous inside the body)

phrases.english: Rav said to his son Chiyya,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הוּנָא לְרַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ:
phrases.english: and Rav Huna likewise said to his son Rabba:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל מִידַּעַם לָא תִּפְלוֹט קַמֵּיהּ רַבָּךְ,
phrases.english: Do not spit out anything in front of your teacher,
except gourd and porridge,
because they are like a wick of lead,
phrases.notes: If these foods are swallowed when they will not go down well, they harm the insides like burning lead.

phrases.english: and spit them out even in front of King Shapur.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל מִידַּעַם לָא תִּפְלוֹט קַמֵּיהּ רַבָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from the same pair of fathers, again mentioning porridge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not spit food out before your teacher, except gourd and porridge, which you should spit out even before a king because of the danger.

steps.title: Fingers or fork: the fork-eater complains
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי and רבי יהודה eat porridge together, one with his fingers and one with a fork. The fork-eater complains that he is being fed the other's dirt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי and רבי יהודה: one ate porridge with his fingers, and one ate with a fork. The one eating with a fork said to the one eating with his fingers: How long will you feed me your filth?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins about table manners. One rabbi teases the other for putting his fingers into the shared dish, and the story sets up the reply that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both men eat from one bowl. The fork-eater says that fingers bring dirt from under the nails into the shared food. This ties back to step 9, where רב הונא ate porridge with his fingers.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda:
one ate porridge with his fingers,
and one ate with a fork.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ דְּאָכֵיל בְּהוּצָא לִדְאָכֵיל בְּאֶצְבְּעָתֵיהּ:
phrases.english: The one eating with a fork said to the one eating with his fingers:
How long will you feed me your filth!
phrases.notes: He means the dirt under the fingernails that gets into the shared bowl.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, חַד אָכֵיל דַּיְיסָא בְּאֶצְבְּעָתֵיהּ וְחַד אָכֵיל בְּהוּצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new porridge story about how to eat it, connecting to רב הונא eating with his fingers in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating with your fingers from a shared bowl can be seen as putting dirt into other people's food.

steps.title: The finger-eater answers back
steps.stepSummary: The finger-eater replies that the fork-eater is feeding him spit, since the fork goes from his mouth back into the bowl.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one eating with his fingers said to the one eating with a fork: How long will you feed me your spit!
steps.whatsHappening: The finger-eater turns the complaint around: the fork is not cleaner either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fork goes into the mouth and then back into the shared bowl, carrying saliva with it. So each method has its own problem, and the story ends with the two of them even.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ דְּאָכֵיל בְּאֶצְבְּעָתֵיהּ לִדְאָכֵיל בְּהוּצָא:
phrases.english: The one eating with his fingers said to the one eating with a fork:
How long will you feed me your spit!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ דְּאָכֵיל בְּאֶצְבְּעָתֵיהּ לִדְאָכֵיל בְּהוּצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the complaint of step 12 by pointing out the same kind of problem with a fork.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A fork is no better, because it carries saliva from the mouth back into the shared dish.

steps.title: Why won't you eat the figs?
steps.stepSummary: Figs called בלוספיין are served to רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון. רבי יהודה eats and רבי שמעון does not, so רבי יהודה asks him why.
steps.simpleTranslation: בלוספיין figs were brought before רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון. רבי יהודה ate; רבי שמעון did not eat. רבי יהודה said to him: Why is the Master not eating?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts. It sets up a question about why one rabbi refuses a certain food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two rabbis react differently to the same food. רבי יהודה asks for the reason, which leads into the next two steps.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon:
belospayin figs were brought before them.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אֲכַל, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן לָא אֲכַל.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ate; Rabbi Shimon did not eat.
Rabbi Yehuda said to him:
Why is the Master not eating?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new food story, this time about figs rather than porridge.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason רבי שמעון refuses to eat the בלוספיין.

steps.title: These figs never leave the stomach
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון explains that these figs do not pass out of the intestines at all, meaning they are very hard to digest.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said to him: These do not leave the intestines at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון gives his reason: the figs stay in the body and do not digest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, a food that sits in the intestines without digesting is unhealthy, so he avoids it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אֵלּוּ אֵין יוֹצְאִין מִבְּנֵי מֵעַיִם כׇּל עִיקָּר.
phrases.english: These do not leave the intestines at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵלּוּ אֵין יוֹצְאִין מִבְּנֵי מֵעַיִם כׇּל עִיקָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The figs are not digested; they stay in the intestines.

steps.title: All the better: they will fill us up tomorrow
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה turns the reason around: if the figs stay inside, they will keep us full into tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said to him: All the more so, since we can rely on them for tomorrow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה takes רבי שמעון's own reason and makes it a reason to eat the figs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון saw slow digestion as a problem. רבי יהודה sees it as an advantage: food that stays inside keeps a person full, so one meal can carry him into the next day.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said to him:
All the more so, since we can rely on them for tomorrow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reason given in step 15 by turning it into a reason to eat.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי שמעון's reason for not eating.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Slow digestion is not only a drawback; it also keeps a person full longer.

steps.title: רבי טרפון notices רבי יהודה's healthy face
steps.stepSummary: While רבי יהודה sits before רבי טרפון, רבי טרפון remarks that his face looks rosy and healthy today.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה was sitting before רבי טרפון. רבי טרפון said to him: Today your face is glowing.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts. רבי טרפון's remark sets up רבי יהודה's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The remark works as a hidden question: what made you look so healthy? It sets the stage for the beets.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הֲוָה יָתֵיב קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי טַרְפוֹן.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda was sitting before Rabbi Tarfon.
Rabbi Tarfon said to him:
Today your face is glowing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about רבי יהודה and a healthy food.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי טרפון observes that רבי יהודה looks unusually healthy.

steps.title: Beets made our faces healthy
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה explains that last night the students ate beets without salt. With salt, their faces would have looked even healthier.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Last night your servants went out to the field and brought us beets, and we ate them without salt. Had we eaten them with salt, our faces would have glowed even more.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה answers רבי טרפון: the beets they ate are the reason for his healthy look.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Beets are presented as a healthy food. Even plain beets without salt did this much, so with salt the effect would have been even greater.
steps.whatToRemember: These stories praise certain foods (porridge, ox meat, beets) and warn about others (gourd, hard figs). Each one mixes health advice with good manners.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Last night your servants went out to the field,
phrases.notes: A humble way of saying 'we, your students'.

phrases.english: and brought us beets,
and we ate them without salt.
And had we eaten them with salt,
all the more so our faces would have glowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the healthy look that רבי טרפון noticed in step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Eating beets, even without salt, gave them a healthy face; with salt it would have been even more so.

steps.title: A noblewoman accuses רבי יהודה of drinking
steps.stepSummary: A noblewoman sees רבי יהודה's rosy face and mocks him: how can a teacher also be a drunk?
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain noblewoman said to רבי יהודה: A teacher and a drunk?
steps.whatsHappening: A non-Jewish noblewoman sees רבי יהודה's rosy face. She assumes he drinks a lot of wine and challenges him for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This picks up the theme from the last steps, where רבי טרפון said רבי יהודה's face looked healthy. Here someone reads that same rosy face as a sign of drinking. Her words sound like a question, but they are really an accusation that he is a hypocrite.

keyTerms.meaning: A noblewoman, an important non-Jewish lady
A teacher, someone who rules on halacha

phrases.english: A certain noblewoman said to רבי יהודה:
A teacher and a drunk?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the stories about רבי יהודה's healthy-looking face, now told by an outsider who gives it a negative reason.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's credibility as a teacher
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rosy face suggests heavy drinking, and a drunk cannot properly teach and rule.

steps.title: רבי יהודה swears he barely drinks and credits his wisdom
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה swears he drinks wine only for קידוש, הבדלה, and the four cups of פסח, and even those give him a headache until שבועות. His glow comes from wisdom, as the פסוק says.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: You can stop trusting me if I taste any wine besides קידוש, הבדלה, and the four cups of פסח. And I have to bind my temples from פסח until שבועות. Rather, the reason is: "A man's wisdom lights up his face."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה strongly denies that he drinks. He explains that his face shines because of his Torah wisdom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He first rejects her reason: he drinks only the wine of a מצוה, and even that hurts him for weeks. Then he gives a different reason for his glow, using a פסוק that says wisdom makes a person's face shine.

keyTerms.meaning: קידוש and הבדלה, the wine at the start and end of שבת
My temples, the sides of the forehead

phrases.english: He said to her:
My trustworthiness is in the hands of this woman,
if I taste anything except קידוש and הבדלה
and the four cups of פסח,

phrases.aramaic: וְחוֹגְרַנִי צִידְעַי מִן הַפֶּסַח עַד הָעֲצֶרֶת,
phrases.english: and I bind my temples from פסח until שבועות,
phrases.notes: Those four cups give him a headache so bad that he wraps his head for weeks.

phrases.english: Rather: "A man's wisdom lights up his face."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לַהּ: הֵימָנוּתָא בִּידָא דְּהָהִיא אִיתְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the noblewoman's accusation.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He hardly drinks at all. His shining face comes from Torah wisdom.

steps.title: A heretic says רבי יהודה looks like a lender or a pig farmer
steps.stepSummary: A heretic insults רבי יהודה, saying his face looks like the face of people who lend with interest or raise pigs.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic said to רבי יהודה: Your face looks either like the face of people who lend with interest or like the face of people who raise pigs.
steps.whatsHappening: A second outsider gives a different insulting reason for רבי יהודה's healthy face. This time the claim is that he lives off easy money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The insult suggests that רבי יהודה is well-fed because he earns easily, without hard work. Both jobs he names are forbidden to Jews, so the remark also hints that he is doing something wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: A heretic, someone who denies the Torah
People who lend money with interest

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to רבי יהודה:
Your face looks either like the face of those who lend with interest
or like the face of those who raise pigs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second accusation about the same rosy face, this time from a heretic.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's honesty in how he makes a living
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A well-fed look suggests easy money, and the easy jobs he names are forbidden ones.

steps.title: רבי יהודה says both jobs are forbidden and gives a bodily reason
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה answers that Jews are forbidden to do both jobs. His face is healthy because he has 24 bathrooms on his way to the בית מדרש, and he uses every one of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: For Jews, both of these are forbidden. Rather, I have twenty-four bathrooms between my house and the בית מדרש, and every time I go, I enter each and every one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה rejects the heretic's claim. He explains that his healthy look comes from his body working well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First he knocks out both suggestions, since a Jew may not do either job. Then he gives a physical reason: his digestion works smoothly, which keeps him looking healthy. This connects back to the figs story, where food that does not pass through the body was a concern.

keyTerms.meaning: The בית מדרש, the study hall

phrases.english: He said to him: For Jews, both of them are forbidden.
Rather, twenty-four bathrooms

phrases.aramaic: אִית לִי מִן בֵּיתָא עַד בֵּי מִדְרְשָׁא,
phrases.english: I have between my house and the study hall,
and every single time
I go into each and every one of them.
phrases.notes: His body works smoothly and he is never stopped up, and that is what keeps him looking healthy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the heretic's insult.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Both jobs are forbidden to Jews. His healthy look comes from good digestion.

steps.title: רבי יהודה carries a jug and praises work
steps.stepSummary: On his way to the בית מדרש, רבי יהודה carries a jug on his shoulder and says that work is great because it honors the one who does it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יהודה went to the בית מדרש, he would carry a jug on his shoulder. He said: Work is great, because it brings honor to the one who does it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about רבי יהודה. He carries his own jug to the בית מדרש and praises work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carrying the jug is plain physical labor. Yet it gives him something respectable to sit on in the בית מדרש. That is how the work 'honors' the one who does it.

keyTerms.meaning: Its owner, the one who does it

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה כַּד אָזֵיל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא
phrases.english: רבי יהודה, when he would go to the study hall,
would carry a jug on his shoulder,
saying: Work is great,
because it honors the one who does it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה כַּד אָזֵיל לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from stories about his face to a new story about his attitude toward work.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Work is great because it brings honor to the person who does it.

steps.title: רבי שמעון carries a basket and says the same thing
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון also carries something on his shoulder, a basket, and says the very same words about the greatness of work.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון would carry a basket on his shoulder. He said: Work is great, because it brings honor to the one who does it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a matching story about רבי שמעון. He carries a basket and praises work in the same words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repeated wording shows that both תנאים shared the same value. Both saw even simple labor as something dignified, and neither felt it was beneath them.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן שָׁקֵיל צַנָּא עַל כַּתְפֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: רבי שמעון would carry a basket on his shoulder,
saying: Work is great,
because it honors the one who does it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן שָׁקֵיל צַנָּא עַל כַּתְפֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to רבי יהודה's, with the same saying.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שמעון also holds that work honors the one who does it.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's wife makes a cloak that they both wear
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה's wife gathers wool and makes a thick cloak. She wears it to the market, and he wears it when he goes out to pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה's wife went out, gathered wool, and made a thick cloak. When she went out to the market, she covered herself with it. When רבי יהודה went out to pray, he would cover himself with it and pray.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about רבי יהודה's home life. His wife makes one cloak, and the two of them take turns wearing it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They had only one good cloak between them, so they shared it. This shows how simply they lived. It also sets up the next step, which shows how he felt about this cloak.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה's wife went out,
gathered wool,
and made a thick cloak.
When she went out to the market, she covered herself with it,
and when רבי יהודה went out to pray,
he would cover himself with it and pray.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about רבי יהודה's home life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה and his wife shared a single homemade cloak.

steps.title: רבי יהודה makes a joyful ברכה on the cloak
steps.stepSummary: Whenever רבי יהודה wrapped himself in the shared cloak, he said the ברכה: Blessed is He who wrapped me in a coat.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he covered himself with it, he would make a ברכה: "Blessed is He who wrapped me in a coat."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the cloak story. Each time רבי יהודה put on the simple shared cloak, he made a ברכה over it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the cloak was plain and shared, he treated it like a fine garment and thanked ה׳ for it. His joy came from appreciating what he had, not from having a lot.
steps.whatToRemember: These stories paint a picture of רבי יהודה. His face shone from wisdom and health, not from wine or forbidden money. He valued simple work, and he joyfully thanked ה׳ even for a plain cloak he shared with his wife.

phrases.english: And when he covered himself with it,
he would make a blessing:
"Blessed is He who wrapped me in a coat."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the cloak story by showing how רבי יהודה felt about the cloak.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה made a ברכה of thanks each time he wore the shared cloak.

steps.title: A public fast is declared and רבי יהודה does not come
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל declares a public fast, and רבי יהודה is missing from the gathering.
steps.simpleTranslation: One time, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל declared a public fast day. רבי יהודה did not come to the place where the fast was held.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new short story about רבי יהודה. It sets the scene: there is a public fast, and רבי יהודה is missing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story builds on the earlier steps showing how poor רבי יהודה was, since he and his wife shared one cloak. Here his poverty shows up in public, because he does not come to a community event. The story does not yet say why he stayed away.

keyTerms.meaning: The place of the fast, where the community gathered to pray

phrases.english: One time, decreed
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel a fast,
Rabbi Yehuda did not come
to the house of the fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: זִימְנָא חֲדָא גְּזַר רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל תַּעֲנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the stories about רבי יהודה's poverty, after the step about the one cloak he shared with his wife.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: During a public fast declared by רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, רבי יהודה did not come to the gathering.

steps.title: People explain he has nothing proper to wear
steps.stepSummary: People tell רבן שמעון בן גמליאל that רבי יהודה stayed away because he has no proper garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: They told him: He does not have a proper garment to cover himself with.
steps.whatsHappening: People explain to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל why רבי יהודה did not come: he has no decent clothing to wear in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains the absence from the step before. It ties back to step 25, where רבי יהודה and his wife shared a single cloak. If she was using it, or it was not fit for a public gathering, he had nothing respectable to wear.

phrases.english: They said to him:
He does not have a covering.
phrases.notes: This is talking about רבי יהודה: he has no proper garment to wear in public.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִין לֵיהּ: לָא אִית לֵיהּ כִּסּוּיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason רבי יהודה was missing from the fast in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה was absent because he had no proper garment.

steps.title: A cloak is sent, but רבי יהודה refuses it
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל sends רבי יהודה a cloak, but רבי יהודה does not accept it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל sent him a cloak, and רבי יהודה did not accept it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל tries to solve the problem by sending a cloak. רבי יהודה turns it down, and the story is set up to continue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You would expect a poor man to gladly take the gift, so the refusal is surprising. The גמרא has not yet said why he refused. That is the next move in the story.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not guess the reason for the refusal yet. The text here only says he refused, and the explanation comes next.

phrases.english: He sent him a cloak
and he did not accept.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the problem in step 28 (no garment) with a gift, which רבי יהודה refuses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה refused the cloak sent by רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
